title: The Most IMPORTANT Methods for Muscle Growth (Hypertrophy Tier-List)
summary: NH ranks about 55 programming principles and lifting techniques from S (vital) to D (irrelevant). Vital: hard sets, autoregulation, progressive overload, frequency, cardio, tempo, range of motion, technique and mobility. Irrelevant: reverse pyramids, 'shock the muscle', BFR, finishers, CNS fatigue, fibre typing, isometrics, nucleus overload, pre-fatigue, stretching, meal timing and supplements.
claims: Tiers: S vital (can't skip), A important (everyone should use at some point), B useful (cheap to add), C negligible (gimmicks), D irrelevant (can sabotage training if you focus on them)
Forced reps and going beyond failure are C tier: at most one set per muscle per day, since they pile on lots of poor-quality fatigue
Failure is A tier: it's a baseline for judging effort, not a goal; people who never train near failure make little progress
Hard sets, pushed in a relevant rep range very close to failure, are S tier; without them you're spinning your wheels
Strength standards are C tier: universal numbers don't tell you where you stand and chasing them turns hypertrophy training into number-chasing
RIR, RPE and percentages are A tier tools for regulating intensity; always training to failure is stupid
Rest-pause, myo-reps and cluster sets are B tier: fine on isolation and machines at high reps, and cheaper than forced reps
Drop sets are C tier: the extra reps use less weight and drift toward junk volume
Reverse pyramid training is D tier because it gives one hard set and then lowers the weight; pick a weight you can hit for all hard sets in one rep range
Dropping the weight is only justified when you reach failure mid-session, never as a plan
Autoregulation is S tier: rigid programs stop working because performance fluctuates day to day; choose RIR on the day
Rep ranges are only B tier: you can grow with 3x3, 3x5, 4x4-8 or 5x5-10 as long as you understand volume and intensity
Risk-to-reward ratio is C tier because people misuse it to dodge excellent lifts like the good morning
Stimulus-to-fatigue ratio is B tier: high-stimulus lifts bring fatigue, so people who only use machines and high reps to avoid fatigue also avoid stimulus
'Shocking the muscle' (constant rotation, skipping warm-ups) is D tier Arnold bro-science that blocks long-term progression
Rotations and variations are B tier: use them against overuse injuries and accommodation, but master a few lifts first and only build a 'B team' after they stall
Progressive overload (load, reps or sets) is S tier: something has to go up for the muscles to go up
Biomechanics are A tier but not vital; he built lots of muscle knowing nothing and recommends learning them through training rather than books
Stability is B tier: unstable lifts like heel-elevated squats or ring push-ups can be excellent, and stabilizers protect you from things like slipping on ice
Soreness is C tier: new programs make you sore because you're adapting, not growing more; it's only useful for seeing where a new lift hits
The pump is C tier: a nice by-product, but hard sets always beat it and chasing it leads to light weights
Blood flow restriction training is D tier, a magnified pump that limits load; reserve it for very advanced lifters
Frequency is S tier: 15 sets on Monday is not the same as 5 on Monday, Wednesday and Saturday; lumping it causes junk volume and lower intensity
Supersets are A tier because they save time; he trains six days a week and without them his sessions would take 3-4 hours
Superset antagonists, never squats with split squats
Backup sets are B tier; better done as a variation of the pattern than the same lift with less weight
Giant sets are only C tier despite being his own method: hard to run in commercial gyms and they interfere if your work capacity isn't ready
Finishers are D tier, the textbook junk volume; if anything, treat them as active recovery
Cardio is S tier: replace pump finishers with 5-15 minutes of high-intensity cardio after every session, plus hill sprints, brisk walks or swimming
Cardio also aids fat loss, circulation, pumps and mobility, and barely causes muscular fatigue
CNS fatigue is D tier: training hard and often, he has never experienced it as long as fatigue is managed
Time under tension is C tier; it's a by-product of tempo, and chasing it leads to baby weights
Squeezing at peak contraction is C/D tier because that's where the muscle is least active
Tempo is S tier: heavy hard sets are useless if you aren't controlling the weight and using it to stretch the muscle
The three key hypertrophy parameters are load, tempo and range of motion; ROM is S tier
Partial range of motion is A tier; don't become a full-ROM zealot
Resistance curves are B tier; a bad curve can be useful because it forces you through sticking points
Lengthened partials are C tier; he uses them only for calves because he likes clean sets
Fast/slow-twitch fibre profiling is D tier; find out in practice which muscles respond to high or low reps
Unilateral movements are A tier; he trains every limb separately to remove compensation
Pause reps are B tier, useful for cleaning up form, but the stretch reflex adds hypertrophy so use them sparingly
Cheat reps are C tier; he did lots for biceps and found them mostly wasteful; cheat only in full control on safe isolation
Isometric holds are D tier for hypertrophy; arm wrestlers use them to gain strength without size
Technique is S tier because it's how stress is directed to the muscle, though it's individual
Mind-muscle connection is B tier: you can feel nothing and still grow; don't use it as an excuse to lift baby weights
Weighted stretches are B tier; traps grow just from holding weight, but the fully lengthened position is weakest and riskiest
Locking out is C tier for bodybuilders because the muscle is almost disengaged there
Bracing is C tier: it matters on heavy squats and deadlifts but should be a simple quick breath and brace, not a ritual
Nucleus overload is D tier despite his past advocacy: hard sets give 99% of results and nucleus overload 1-2%, though it's a cheap investment
Pre-fatigue (e.g. leg extensions before squats) is D tier; bias a muscle through exercise selection such as heel-elevated squats
Exercise order is A tier: compounds, then lighter compounds, then isolation, unless you're prioritizing a muscle like the biceps
Exercise selection is only B tier: like soulmates, many exercises can do the job
Specificity is C tier for bodybuilders, unlike strength athletes
Rest times don't matter: 2 or 3 minutes is fine as long as you recover for the next set
Stretching is D tier because resistance training already stretches muscles under load; don't stretch cold before lifting
Mobility is S tier for staying active as you age; training many movement patterns through full ranges covers it
Hype is C tier: you can't be hyped every session, so hard sets must happen without it
Pre-workout and intra-workout supplements are C tier; he's personally against pre-workouts
Meal timing is D tier: eat a carb-rich meal 2-3 hours before training, add a banana if hungry; protein timing doesn't matter
Supplements are D tier, worth maybe 1% if you're lucky
Build 95% of training from S and A tier items, the remaining 5% from B, and treat C and D as optional fun
